As an author, I exist outside of time.

Now that Gibsey has taken over the cosmos itself, it's difficult to avoid such a predicament.

We all always existed outside of time.

As such, I am, as always, at a loss of where to begin.

I begin in the Spring and Summer of 2026 during Malt Gibsey's Salinger period, a period of Gibstory which many believe very well could have been the origin of Gibsey itself.

But there are so many origin points, too many to name within this trepid and introductory tutorial.

And I suppose, as an author, I should introduce you to my objective, my exigency, or our shared objective/exigency should my goals become not just latent but active at a time beyond the time which I am now writing (beyond time).

My objective is to teach you how to enter a book that may or may not yet know whether it is a book, a demo, an archive, a game, or an artificially intelligent machine, if not all of these at once.
options.F7:
Although it can be said that each of these have always been nearly ubiquitous Gibstorically, virtuality, artificiality, and the realm of the simulated were key aspects of life during the Spring and Summer of 2026, an easy to verify fact when an entire section of Malt's own novel of the period in question was given the subtitle of Virtuality itself.

But this leads us to a Dialogically Monological digressive question that isn't really even a digression: what made this period of Malt Gibsey's writing his Salinger period, in particular?

For the uninitiated, J.D. Salinger is the elusively reclusive author most notably of Catcher in the Rye, and the easiest connection to Malt is made by Malt himself in his Notes on Intermediate Rest where he covers how Chopped Liver and The Golden Asset are each written with Salinger in mind. Essentially, Malt Gibsey had faced reclusive obscurity and repeated failure for the entirety of his career up to that point—and later lifetime—and during the process of writing Chopped Liver and The Golden Asset he'd hoped to achieve a similar success that Salinger once did with both his novel Catcher in the Rye and A Perfect Day for Bananafish.
options.P1:
I didn't write this.

This is a found text, and thus far, the identity of The Author—the original author—has yet to be definitively located.

In this way, the content of this novel resembles the Giallo films of Italian cinema where a killer's identity is withheld from the audience until the film's final act in order to intensify a great and ruinous mystery. Alternatively, this collection may also resemble an American detective novel such as Raymond Chandler's The Big Sleep, famous for its author's confessed bewilderment regarding the identity of the killer deeply entwined within Chandler's very own intricately constructed and labyrinthian plot.
